{"mode": "worked-example", "text": "Worked example: Determine whether {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} is linearly independent. Set up a linear combination a(1,0)+b(0,1)+c(1,1)=(0,0). This gives equations a+c=0 and b+c=0. Choose c=1, then a=-1 and b=-1 to get a nontrivial solution, so the set is dependent. Connect directly to the misconception: distinct vectors can still be dependent."}

Worked example (using the standard independence test): Let v1=(1,0) and v2=(0,1) in R^2. Check a linear combination a v1 + b v2 = 0. That becomes (a, b) = (0,0), so a=0 and b=0. Only the trivial combination gives 0, so {v1,v2} is linearly independent. Now connect to dependence: if instead we used v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), v3=(1,1), then v3 = v1+v2 gives a nontrivial combination a v1 + b v2 + c v3 = 0, so the set is dependent.

Worked example (vector-space vs. not): Let S = {(a,b) ∈ R^2 : a + b = 1}. Test the subspace conditions (using the vector-space axioms idea): does S contain the zero vector? Conclude: S is not a vector space (and hence not a subspace of R^2).

{"text": "Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector\u2014polynomials, matrices, and functions included\u2014so geometry is one model, not the definition. In R\u00b3, this is why every (a,b,c) can be written as (a,b,0) + (0,0,c), making the sum span all of R\u00b3. If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence."}

Parallel vectors do not give a two-dimensional span; the span can be a line, and if one vector is zero it can collapse further. The size of the span depends on independence, not on whether the vectors are different. Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness. Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent; adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it. Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.

{"text": "In R^2, consider v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), and v3=(1,1). Which statement is correct?
They are independent because the vectors are different from each other.
They are dependent because v3 is a linear combination of v1 and v2.

Distinct vectors can still be dependent—for example, (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet satisfy (1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1). Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent; adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it.

{"text": "Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and the call stack overflows. The fix also requires that recursion shrink the input rather than repeatedly making the same-size call. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class."}

Without a base case, the self-calls have no stopping point, so recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack. The correct fix is to add the simplest input solved directly without another call. A class is the blueprint; you create instances from it (e.g. d = Dog()), and per-object data lives on each instance, not on the class. Each instance has its own attributes, so changing one Dog's name does not change another Dog's name; only the methods are shared. Each recursive call must move toward the base case by shrinking the problem (e.g. n - 1), or the base case is never reached.

{"text": "The loop variable x is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, you would need to index into the list directly. This is the case where the belief that reassigning the loop variable changes the underlying list is wrong. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value."}

The loop variable is a fresh binding to each element in turn; assigning to it does not edit the container. To change list contents, index into the list directly. Reassigning the loop variable inside a for loop does not change the underlying list it came from. Local variables exist only during the call that created them; to use a result outside, the function must return it and the caller must capture the returned value. Every while loop must change something the condition depends on; a counter loop needs n = n - 1 (or += 1) inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false. The loop expression is tested only at the top of each iteration; the rest of the current pass still runs before the condition is checked again.
